claims.text: kubectl cordon marks a node unschedulable (spec.unschedulable: true): the scheduler places no new Pod there, except DaemonSet Pods, which tolerate it; Pods already on it keep running; kubectl uncordon clears the mark.
claims.source_hint: refs/kubernetes-website content/en/docs/concepts/architecture/nodes.md lines 152-168 (unschedulable, DaemonSet note); outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/drain.txt lines 1-11

claims.text: kubectl drain first cordons the node, then evicts its Pods through the Eviction API; their controllers (the object that created a Pod and replaces it, such as the ReplicaSet of a Deployment) recreate them, and the scheduler avoids the cordoned node.
claims.source_hint: kubectl drain reference line 29; safely-drain-node.md; disruptions.md lines 111-116; concepts/architecture/controller.md; drain.txt line 23

claims.text: An eviction is a request to the API server to delete a Pod that the API server checks first (against PodDisruptionBudgets) and may refuse, unlike a direct delete.
claims.source_hint: concepts/scheduling-eviction/api-eviction.md (429 Too Many Requests, line 75); disruptions.md lines 62-64

claims.text: Without flags, kubectl drain evicts nothing if the node runs DaemonSet-managed Pods (--ignore-daemonsets), Pods with emptyDir (--delete-emptydir-data) or Pods with no controller (--force), and lists them; its message for the last repeats 'cannot delete'.
claims.source_hint: kubectl drain reference (flags --ignore-daemonsets, --delete-emptydir-data, --force) lines 29, 68-71, 89-92; drain.txt lines 13-16

claims.text: DaemonSet Pods (one per node, such as kindnet, kind's CNI plugin) would be recreated at once on the same node: the DaemonSet controller replaces missing Pods and ignores the unschedulable mark.
claims.source_hint: kubectl drain reference line 29; safely-drain-node.md lines 85-90; k8s.l3.cni-plugins claims (kindnet is kind's CNI plugin)

claims.text: An emptyDir is a scratch folder whose data is deleted when its Pod leaves the node; a Pod with no controller evicted with --force is not recreated by anything.
claims.source_hint: concepts/storage/volumes.md lines 163-167; kubectl drain reference lines 89-92 (--force)

claims.text: A PodDisruptionBudget (policy/v1) selects Pods with a label selector and sets minAvailable or maxUnavailable; the API server refuses an eviction that would break it.
claims.source_hint: tasks/run-application/configure-pdb.md lines 110-111, 125; api-eviction.md lines 75-76; deploy/k8s/lessons/web-pdb.yaml @ stage-3

claims.text: PDB status counts selected Ready Pods (readiness probe passes; no probe counts as success, so running containers suffice); the API server checks it per eviction. 3 ready, minAvailable 2 (or maxUnavailable 1): one eviction at a time. minAvailable = replicas allows none.
claims.source_hint: configure-pdb.md lines 157-158, 210-240 (healthy = Ready, currentHealthy); probes.md line 205 (no probe = Success); safely-drain-node.md lines 109-117; drain.txt lines 20-55

claims.text: kubectl drain retries evictions refused by a budget until all Pods are gone or its --timeout is reached; --timeout 0 (the default) means it retries forever. In the lab it printed 'will retry after 5s' and 'global timeout reached: 30s'.
claims.source_hint: disruptions.md lines 111-116; kubectl drain reference lines 137-141 (--timeout, zero means infinite); drain.txt lines 27 and 48

claims.text: Involuntary disruptions such as a node failure cannot be prevented by PDBs but count against the budget (fewer available, so it allows fewer evictions, or none, until replacements are ready); rolling updates of Deployments are not limited by PDBs, their own spec governs them.
A direct kubectl delete pod is not an eviction, so a PodDisruptionBudget does not hold it back; in the lab it succeeded under minAvailable 3 of 3.
kubectl drain --pod-selector limits the drain to Pods matching the label selector, so other Pods on the node (including ones that would block a plain drain) are left alone.
claims.source_hint: kubectl drain reference lines 116-120 (--pod-selector); drain.txt lines 13-32

claims.text: kubectl create deployment web labels its Pods app=web, which the budget's selector matches. In drain.sh, show prints then runs a command, pods lists Pods with status and node, drain prints each repeated line once.
claims.source_hint: debug-service.md lines 87-88; drain.sh lines 15, 18-20 @ stage-3; scripts/lib/network-lessons.sh (show)

claims.text: A Pod whose claim is on kind's standard class (rancher.io/local-path) is tied to the node holding the folder: after a drain it stays Pending with no node until that node is uncordoned. store is a one-replica Deployment with no budget.
claims.source_hint: persistent-volumes.md lines 739-741 (PV node affinity); local-path-provisioner README; drain.sh lines 72-105 @ stage-3; drain.txt lines 61-72

claims.text: Draining the node of a single-copy store whose volume lives on that node is an outage; if an application must keep serving during maintenance, it needs a second replica on another node.
claims.source_hint: outline items 6 and misconception 2; disruptions.md line 72

claims.text: Lab, web-pdb.yaml: three evictions requested, two refused and retried, drain ended node/donhang-worker drained. Before the strict drain, drain.sh deletes the web Pods on donhang-worker2, then cordons it until replacements are ready; two of three were then on donhang-worker.
